\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:ka-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a Kannada verb as stem plus tense plus person, swap the middle bead for the past, hear the p $\to$ h law that separates Kannada from its three sisters, and say why \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} carries no person at all.}

Say \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು}, name the three slots that built iruttēne, hōguttēne and nōḍuttēne, explain which slot \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} leaves empty and where its person went instead, and give the sound-law behind pōgu $\to$ hōgu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[iru]{\kn{ಇರು} (iru) — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the machine inside every Kannada verb}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-iru}



\begin{quote}
Thirty-one chapters of words. Now the engine room. Kannada builds a verb the way you thread beads on a string, and this first verb carries the whole string.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಇರು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಇರು}} — \emph{iru} — \textbf{to be, to exist, to stay, to live}
\end{quote}

It is native Dravidian, from an old root meaning \textquotedblleft{}be, remain, stay put.\textquotedblright{} Tamil kept the very same word, \textbf{\ta{இரு}} (\emph{iru}), and Malayalam has \textbf{\ml{ഇരിക്കുക}} (\emph{irikkuka}); Telugu went its own way with \textbf{\te{ఉండు}} (\emph{uṇḍu}).

\emph{Iru} is about \textbf{existing} or \textbf{being somewhere}, not about linking two nouns: \textquotedblleft{}I am in Bangalore\textquotedblright{} takes \emph{iru}, but \textquotedblleft{}I am a teacher\textquotedblright{} takes no verb at all.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\kn{ಇ}} (the standing vowel \emph{i}) + \textbf{\kn{ರು}} (\emph{ru}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಇರು}}. Both shapes turned up already in \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{illa}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}).

The form you hear most is \textbf{\kn{ಇದ್ದೇನೆ}} (\emph{iddēne}), \textquotedblleft{}I am,\textquotedblright{} its \textbf{\kn{ದ್ದ}} held long — \emph{id-dē-ne}. You have said it already, inside Chapter 3's \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ}} (\emph{cennāgiddēne}, \textquotedblleft{}I'm well\textquotedblright{}).
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem, then tense, then person}]
English changes a verb by putting words \textbf{around} it: \emph{I am, I was, I will be}. Kannada changes it by gluing pieces \textbf{onto the end} of it, always in the same order:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಇರು}} + \textbf{\kn{ಉತ್ತ}} + \textbf{\kn{ಏನೆ}} $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಇರುತ್ತೇನೆ}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{iru} (be) + \emph{-utt-} (happening now) + \emph{-ēne} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{iruttēne}
\end{quote}

Left to right: \textbf{be — present — I}, three slots welded into one word. Languages built this way are called \textbf{agglutinative}, from Latin \emph{glutinare}, \textquotedblleft{}to glue.\textquotedblright{}

Two payoffs at once. The last piece already means \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} so \emph{nānu} is optional. And nothing here belongs to \emph{iru} alone: every verb in this chapter is the same three slots with a new first bead.

(\emph{Iruttēne} is the regular build, \textquotedblleft{}I stay, I will be\textquotedblright{}; \emph{iddēne} is the same verb worn down onto its own past stem \emph{idd-}, for \textquotedblleft{}I am \textbf{right now}.\textquotedblright{})
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iru\textquotedblright{} — be, exist, stay
  \item the three beads in order — \textquotedblleft{}iru … utt … ēne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sisters — Tamil \textquotedblleft{}iru\textquotedblright{}, Malayalam \textquotedblleft{}irikkuka\textquotedblright{}, Telugu \textquotedblleft{}uṇḍu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three pieces of \emph{iruttēne}, in order? (\textbf{Stem, tense, person} — \emph{iru}, \emph{-utt-}, \emph{-ēne}.) Which piece carries \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{The last one}, \emph{-ēne} — which is why \emph{nānu} can be dropped.) Which sister kept the same verb unchanged, and which went its own way? (\textbf{Tamil} \emph{iru}; \textbf{Telugu} \emph{uṇḍu}.) Next: the sound-law that made Kannada sound unlike all three of its sisters.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hōgu]{\kn{ಹೋಗು} (hōgu) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and the law that made Kannada sound like Kannada}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-hoogu}



\begin{quote}
Keep the three beads and change only the first, and you have a new verb. But this first bead hides the single most useful sound-fact in the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹೋಗು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗು}} — \emph{hōgu} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\kn{ಹೋ}} (\emph{ha} carrying the long-\emph{ō} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ಗು}} (\emph{gu}). Thread the beads and you get \textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\emph{hōguttēne}), \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hōgu} + \emph{-utt-} + \emph{-ēne}, exactly the machine \emph{iru} just handed you. The bare stem is already a command: \emph{hōgu!}, \textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
Tamil's word for \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\ta{போ}} / \textbf{\ta{போகு}} (\emph{pō} / \emph{pōgu}). Kannada's is \emph{hōgu}, and that \emph{h} is \textbf{not} a different root. Around a thousand years ago Kannada softened every old word-initial \emph{\textbf{p-}} to \textbf{h-} — and Kannada is the \textbf{only} one of the four literary Dravidian languages that did it.

Once you know the law, whole shelves of vocabulary line up:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{pōgu} & \emph{hōgu} & go \\
\emph{pattu} & \emph{hattu} & ten \\
\emph{pāl} & \emph{hālu} & milk \\
\emph{peyar} & \emph{hesaru} & name \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have met two of those already — \emph{hattu} in Chapter 7, \emph{hesaru} back in Chapter 2. One law, and both of them stop being coincidences.

The other two sisters kept the \emph{p}: Telugu \textbf{\te{పోవు}} (\emph{pōvu}), \textbf{\te{పది}} (\emph{padi}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{\te{పాలు}} (\emph{pālu}, \textquotedblleft{}milk\textquotedblright{}); Malayalam \textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} (\emph{pōkuka}), \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (\emph{pattu}), \textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} (\emph{pāl}). A whole stripe of the family vocabulary, explained by one change only Kannada made.

The proof is written down: \textbf{Old Kannada} still spells these words with \textbf{\kn{ಪ}} (\emph{pa}), and the modern \emph{h} is the later step. Nor has the law finished — in casual speech many speakers drop the \emph{h} too, so \emph{hōgu} can come out as \emph{ōgu}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hōgu\textquotedblright{} — go — then \textquotedblleft{}hōguttēne\textquotedblright{}, I go
  \item the three beads again — \textquotedblleft{}hōgu … utt … ēne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four pairs — \textquotedblleft{}pōgu … hōgu\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}pattu … hattu\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}pāl … hālu\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}peyar … hesaru\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sisters that kept the p — Telugu \textquotedblleft{}pōvu\textquotedblright{}, Malayalam \textquotedblleft{}pōkuka\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is Kannada's \emph{hōgu} a different root from Tamil's \emph{pōgu}? (\textbf{No} — the same old \emph{p}, softened to \emph{h}.) How many of the four sisters made that change? (\textbf{One} — Kannada alone.) Give two more pairs that follow the law. (\emph{Pattu / hattu}, \emph{pāl / hālu}, \emph{peyar / hesaru}.) What do Old Kannada texts write instead of \kn{ಹ}? (\textbf{\kn{ಪ}}, \emph{pa}.) Build \textquotedblleft{}I go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hōguttēne}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bā / baru]{\kn{ಬಾ} (bā) — \textquotedblleft{}come,\textquotedblright{} and the stem hiding underneath it}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-baa}



\begin{quote}
Every verb so far has been honest: the word you learn it by is the word the endings glue onto. This one is not — and Chapter 4's goodbye has been quietly showing you why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬಾ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಾ}} — \emph{bā} — \textbf{come!}
\end{quote}

One letter and a vowel sign: \textbf{\kn{ಬ}} (\emph{ba}) with the long-\emph{ā} stroke. As it stands it is a whole command — \emph{bā!}, \textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{} — the partner of \emph{hōgu!} from Chapter 4.

But you cannot thread beads onto \emph{bā}. Underneath, the verb's working stem is \textbf{\kn{ಬರು}-} (\emph{baru-}), and everything attaches to that:

\begin{quote}
\emph{baru-} + \emph{-utt-} + \emph{-ēne} $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\emph{baruttēne}), \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two shapes, one verb}]
Most Kannada verbs have nothing to hide. \emph{Iru} gives \emph{iruttēne}, \emph{hōgu} gives \emph{hōguttēne}; the name of the verb \textbf{is} the stem. A small handful do not, and \emph{bā} is the one you will meet daily: \textbf{call it \emph{bā}, build on \emph{baru-}}.

That is exactly what Chapter 4's farewell was made of:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೋಗಿ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ}} — \emph{hōgi baruttēne} — \textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hōgi} is \emph{hōgu} in its \textquotedblleft{}having …-ed\textquotedblright{} form; \emph{baruttēne} is \emph{baru-} with the present bead and the \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} bead. Kannada refuses a bare goodbye, so it promises the return instead — and needs both verbs to do it.

Tamil splits the same verb the same way: \textbf{\ta{வா}} (\emph{vā}) to call it by, \textbf{\ta{வரு}-} (\emph{varu-}) to build on; Malayalam has \textbf{\ml{വരുക}} (\emph{varuka}), Telugu \textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} (\emph{vaccu}), whose command form is \textbf{\te{రా}} (\emph{rā}).

And notice Kannada's \emph{b} against Tamil's \emph{v} — a second Kannada-only habit, sitting right beside the \emph{p} $\to$ \emph{h} law:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{vā} & \emph{bā} & come \\
\emph{vāy} & \emph{bāyi} & mouth \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two laws, both at the front of the word, both Kannada's own. Between them they account for much of why Kannada does not sound like its sisters.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bā\textquotedblright{} — come! — then the stem, \textquotedblleft{}baru-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}baruttēne\textquotedblright{} — I come
  \item the farewell, taken apart — \textquotedblleft{}hōgi … baruttēne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two Kannada laws together — \textquotedblleft{}vā … bā\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pōgu … hōgu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You call this verb \emph{bā} — so what do the endings actually attach to? (\textbf{\kn{ಬರು}-}, \emph{baru-}.) Build \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Baruttēne}.) What are the two halves of \emph{hōgi baruttēne}? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Having gone}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I come}\textquotedblright{} — Kannada promises the return instead of saying goodbye.) Kannada has \emph{bā} where Tamil has \emph{vā}: what change is that? (\textbf{Word-initial \emph{v-} became \emph{b-}}.) Next: the middle bead.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tinnu]{\kn{ತಿನ್ನು} (tinnu) — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} and the bead that carries time}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-tinnu}



\begin{quote}
Hold the first and last beads still and swap only the middle one. That is almost the whole of Kannada tense — almost, because one of the three times you expect is missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ತಿನ್ನು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ತಿನ್ನು}} — \emph{tinnu} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\kn{ತಿ}} (\emph{ta} with the short-\emph{i} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ನ್ನು}} (a doubled \emph{n} with \emph{u}), the \textbf{\kn{ನ್ನ}} held long — \emph{tin-nu}.

It is Proto-Dravidian, an old root meaning simply \textquotedblleft{}eat,\textquotedblright{} and here the family agrees: Telugu \textbf{\te{తిను}} (\emph{tinu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{തിന്നുക}} (\emph{tinnuka}). Tamil has the root as \textbf{\ta{தின்}} (\emph{tiṉ}) — but narrowed it to chewing and snacking, handing everyday eating to \textbf{\ta{சாப்பிடு}} (\emph{sāppiḍu}).

For a \textbf{full meal}, Kannada reaches instead for \textbf{\kn{ಊಟ} \kn{ಮಾಡು}} (\emph{ūṭa māḍu}), \textquotedblleft{}to do a meal\textquotedblright{} — the same noun-plus-\emph{māḍu} trick that built \emph{kelasa māḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} in Chapter 5.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one bead for the past, and a future that never separated}]
Hold the stem \emph{tinn-} and the person bead \emph{-ēne} fixed, and let the middle piece do the work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{Kannada} \\
\midrule
now & \emph{tinnuttēne} \\
already & \emph{tinde} \\
tomorrow & \emph{tinnuttēne} — again \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The past bead is a \textbf{-d-}: \emph{tin} + \emph{-d-} + \emph{-e} $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ತಿಂದೆ}} (\emph{tinde}), \textquotedblleft{}I ate.\textquotedblright{} One consonant of difference between two pieces that never moved. English needs a whole new shape (\emph{ate}); Kannada needs one bead.

Now the surprise in the third row. Everyday Kannada keeps \textbf{no} separate future — the \emph{-utt-} bead covers both:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಳೆ} \kn{ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತೇನೆ}} — \emph{nāḷe tinnuttēne} — \textquotedblleft{}I'll eat \textbf{tomorrow}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The time-word \emph{nāḷe} does the work the verb declines to do. Kannada \textbf{has} a distinct future bead, \emph{-uv-} — \textbf{\kn{ತಿನ್ನುವೆನು}} (\emph{tinnuvenu}) — but you will meet it in writing far more often than in conversation.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tinnu\textquotedblright{} — eat — then \textquotedblleft{}tinnuttēne\textquotedblright{}, I eat
  \item the past — \textquotedblleft{}tinde\textquotedblright{}, I ate
  \item tomorrow, with the same present bead — \textquotedblleft{}nāḷe tinnuttēne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the full meal instead — \textquotedblleft{}ūṭa māḍu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three beads changes for tense? (\textbf{The middle one}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I ate.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Tinde} — the past bead is a \emph{-d-}.) How does everyday Kannada say \textquotedblleft{}I will eat\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{With the present bead}, \emph{tinnuttēne}, plus a time-word like \emph{nāḷe}.) Which sister narrowed this root away from everyday eating? (\textbf{Tamil} — \emph{sāppiḍu} took over.) Next: the third slot, and a word where the four sisters genuinely part company.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nōḍu]{\kn{ನೋಡು} (nōḍu) — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} and the last bead of all}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-noodu}



\begin{quote}
First bead, the verb. Middle bead, the time. One slot is left — the one that lets Kannada drop \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}she\textquotedblright{} altogether.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನೋಡು}} — \emph{nōḍu} — \textbf{to see, to look}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\kn{ನೋ}} (\emph{na} with the long-\emph{ō} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ಡು}} (\emph{ḍu}, tongue curled back — the retroflex \emph{ḍ}, not an English \emph{d}).

\emph{Nōḍu} is native Dravidian, close kin to Tamil's \textbf{\ta{நோக்கு}} (\emph{nōkku}, \textquotedblleft{}to look\textquotedblright{}) — though the exact reconstruction is not fully settled.

What is settled is stranger. Every sister has a native Dravidian everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}see,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{no two chose the same one}: Kannada \textbf{\kn{ನೋಡು}} (\emph{nōḍu}), Tamil \textbf{\ta{பார்}} (\emph{pār}), Telugu \textbf{\te{చూడు}} (\emph{cūḍu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{കാണുക}} (\emph{kāṇuka}). Four inherited roots, one meaning each — a genuine split, like the cat-word in Chapter 21.

And the passed-over roots did not vanish. Kannada still has \textbf{\kn{ಕಾಣು}} (\emph{kāṇu}) — Malayalam's very root — with a different job: \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{appear}, to be visible.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third slot, and where gender lives}]
Hold \emph{nōḍutt-} still and swap only the last bead:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{Kannada} \\
\midrule
I & \emph{nōḍuttēne} \\
you, familiar & \emph{nōḍuttīya} \\
you, respectful & \emph{nōḍuttīri} \\
he & \emph{nōḍuttāne} \\
she & \emph{nōḍuttāḷe} \\
they & \emph{nōḍuttāre} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six endings, and they are not \emph{nōḍu}'s — they are the same six on every verb in this chapter. Learn them once and the other five come free.

Two things worth naming. \textbf{Gender lives only in the third person} — \emph{-āne} he, \emph{-āḷe} she; \emph{nōḍuttēne} is the same word whoever says it. And \textbf{the respectful \emph{-ttīri} is the plural ending}, the same plural-for-respect you met at \emph{nīvu}, sitting inside Chapter 3's \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} (\emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nōḍu\textquotedblright{} — see — then \textquotedblleft{}nōḍuttēne\textquotedblright{}, I see
  \item the six endings — \textquotedblleft{}ēne … īya … īri … āne … āḷe … āre\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four sisters' four see-words — \textquotedblleft{}nōḍu … pār … cūḍu … kāṇuka\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same six beads on another verb — \textquotedblleft{}hōguttēne … hōguttāne … hōguttāre\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which slot does the last bead fill? (\textbf{Person} — which is why the pronoun can be dropped.) In which person does Kannada mark gender? (\textbf{The third} only.) Do the four sisters share an everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — \emph{nōḍu}, \emph{pār}, \emph{cūḍu}, \emph{kāṇuka}, four different native roots.) What job does \emph{kāṇu} do in Kannada? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{appear}.\textquotedblright{}) Next: a know-word with no beads at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gottu]{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} (gottu) — \textquotedblleft{}known,\textquotedblright{} the word with no beads at all}

\label{lesson:KA-C32-gottu}



\begin{quote}
Five verbs, every one ending on a bead that meant \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} The last word of the chapter has no such bead — and Chapter 6 handed you the sentence it makes, whole, before you could take it apart.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತು}} — \emph{gottu} — \textbf{known}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\kn{ಗೊ}} (\emph{ga} with the short-\emph{o} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ತ್ತು}} (a doubled \emph{t} with \emph{u}), the \textbf{\kn{ತ್ತ}} held long — \emph{got-tu}.

And here is the catch: \emph{gottu} is \textbf{not a verb}. It is a noun-like word meaning \textquotedblleft{}known, settled, fixed.\textquotedblright{} No stem slot, no tense bead, no person bead — and it never changes shape.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು}.} — \emph{nanage gottu.} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to-me} {[}it is{]} \textbf{known}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no person slot, so the person moves out}]
Chapter 6 told you \emph{nānu} was gone and the dative \emph{nanage} stood in its place. Now you can see \textbf{why}: a person bead needs a verb to sit on, and \emph{gottu} is not one. So the knower is pushed outside the word entirely:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nanage gottu} — known \textbf{to me}
  \item \emph{ninage gottu} — known \textbf{to you}
  \item \emph{avanige gottu} — known \textbf{to him}
\end{itemize}

Only the little dative word changes. That is the chapter's closing symmetry: five verbs carried the person in the ending, so \emph{nānu} could be dropped; here the ending carries no person, so the dative word is the one thing you \textbf{cannot} drop.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Kannada does have proper verbs for knowing, both native Dravidian. \textbf{\kn{ತಿಳಿ}} (\emph{tiḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}to become clear\textquotedblright{}) takes all three beads — \textbf{\kn{ತಿಳಿಯುತ್ತದೆ}} (\emph{tiḷiyuttade}). \textbf{\kn{ಅರಿ}} (\emph{ari}, \textquotedblleft{}to perceive\textquotedblright{}) survives mostly in writing.

Both have cousins: \emph{tiḷi} answers Tamil \textbf{\ta{தெளி}} (\emph{teḷi}) and Telugu \textbf{\te{తెలియు}} (\emph{teliyu}), everyday form \textbf{\te{తెలుసు}} (\emph{telusu}); \emph{ari} answers Tamil \textbf{\ta{அறி}} (\emph{aṟi}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{അറിയുക}} (\emph{aṟiyuka}). Underneath, this family's word for \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} usually means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{become clear}\textquotedblright{} — and all four sisters put the knower in the dative, exactly as Chapter 6's table showed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gottu\textquotedblright{} — known — then \textquotedblleft{}nanage gottu\textquotedblright{}, I know
  \item the three knowers, one unchanged word — \textquotedblleft{}nanage … ninage … avanige gottu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the five that carried the person — \textquotedblleft{}iruttēne, hōguttēne, baruttēne, tinnuttēne, nōḍuttēne\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{gottu} a verb? (\textbf{No} — a noun-like word meaning \textquotedblleft{}known, settled,\textquotedblright{} with none of the three beads.) So where does the knower go, and why? (\textbf{Into the dative}, \emph{nanage} — there is no person slot for it.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nanage gottu}.) Name the three slots one last time. (\textbf{Stem, tense, person} — \emph{nōḍu} + \emph{-utt-} + \emph{-ēne}.) And the law behind \emph{pōgu} $\to$ \emph{hōgu}? (\textbf{Initial \emph{p-} became \emph{h-}} — in Kannada alone.)
\end{tcolorbox}
